Assessment of the threat from Russia

The security situation has deteriorated further. Russia has intensified
its use of sabotage, destructive cyber attacks and is attacking targets
in Europe with drones. The hybrid war is escalating.

A case in point is the foiled drone attack on the Leipzig/Halle Airport

In Denmark, the Danish Security and Intelligence Service (PET) has
publicly warned that Russia is planning and preparing sabotage on
Danish soil against defence companies.

Russian forces are increasingly acting aggressively towards NATO
military units in the Baltic Sea region. The incident on 14 September
2026, when a Russian frigate in the waters off Gedser fired flares at a
Danish military helicopter is the most recent and most serious example
of such an incident involving Danish military units.

Russia is under pressure

Russia is under more pressure than it has been at any other point
during the war against Ukraine. Ukraine’s sustained long-range attacks
are causing still more extensive damage deep inside Russia. Russia is
suffering heavy losses for marginal territorial gains in Ukraine. At the
same time, the Russian economy is on the brink of a major crisis,
driven by military expenditures, international sanctions and Ukrainian
strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.

Western economic and military support to Ukraine is vital to the
country’s capability to hold back Russian forces and to raise the cost to
Russia of sustaining the war.

There is no prospect of Russia achieving any major breakthroughs in
the war against Ukraine over the next six months. At the same time, it
is highly unlikely that President Putin will be willing to compromise on
his fundamental objectives for the war. Meanwhile, Russia believes that
Europe will gradually develop an autonomous military capability which,
by 2030, will pose an increasing threat to Russia. For Russia, the
coming years therefore present a window of opportunity, during which
President Putin could conclude that it is worth the risk attempting to
drastically change the security order in Europe.

Russia will further escalate its hybrid war
Until recently, Russia’s hybrid attacks against targets in the West have
mainly been aimed at creating fear and weakening public support for
aid to Ukraine. Russia has increasingly begun to directly seek to
prevent support from reaching Ukraine, for instance, by conducting
sabotage against defence companies or against railway transport
carrying military equipment to Ukraine.

The Danish Defence Intelligence Service (DDIS) assesses that Russia
will intensify its hybrid war by carrying out more frequent attacks
against the West and NATO, with greater consequences for the
targeted countries than in the past. This could include destructive cyber
attacks that cripple critical societal functions as well as sabotage
attacks that carry a high risk of casualties.

Risk of Russia launching a limited military attack on one or
several NATO countries
At the same time, there is a low but growing risk that Russia will
launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries
bordering Russia. This could happen even if Russia continues the war
against Ukraine and has not built the military capabilities necessary to
wage a regional war.

A limited military attack would be a desperate move on Russia’s part
and, like the intensified hybrid attacks, could potentially take place in
the coming months. The purpose would be to redirect European
resources away from supporting Ukraine and to sow division within
NATO, should the alliance fail to agree on a collective response.

Such a limited military attack could take the form of isolated strikes
with long-range weapons on infrastructure that is vital to the support to
Ukraine. In this situation, Russia might then claim that the weapons
only struck NATO territory because they were jammed by Ukraine. It
could also be a so-called false flag operation, where Russia uses
Ukrainian-made drones to attack a NATO country.

Russia could also deploy a limited number of military forces, possibly
without national insignia, into NATO countries bordering Russia.
However, ahead of such a deployment, Russia would likely first build up
regular forces near the border in order to be able to counter a potential
NATO response. A build-up of forces would require several months of
preparation and will be difficult to conceal.

Highly unlikely that Russia will launch an invasion
The DDIS still sees no indications that Russia will launch an outright
invasion of one or several NATO countries. Even if Russia decides to
invade a NATO country, it would likely take Russia at least six months
to prepare and build up the necessary forces. Although a Russian
invasion is highly unlikely, it cannot be ruled out.

Russia will likely carry out military attacks only if it assesses that such
attacks will not result in a war by triggering a collective NATO military
response. However, Russia is likely uncertain about what could trigger
such a war. Consequently, there is a risk that Russia assesses that the
NATO countries will not respond collectively, especially if Russia
assesses that the United States cannot or will not support the European
NATO countries in a potential war against Russia.

The updated assessment supplements DDIS’s 9 February 2025
assessment
On 9February 2025, the DDIS published an assessment of the threat
posed by Russia to the Danish Realm, which expanded on a number of
its assessments of the threat from Russia set out in Intelligence
Outlook 2024.

In the February 2025 threat assessment, the DDIS assessed when
Russia could be ready for different types of war. The timelines
depended on that the war in Ukraine ends or turns into a frozen
conflict, that Russia’s conventional military capabilities continue to
grow while the West fails to simultaneously build up its military
capabilities at the same speed, and that Russia assesses that the
United States cannot or will not support the European NATO countries
in a potential war against Russia:

e Within approximately six months, Russia will be able to wage a local
war in a country bordering Russia.

e Within approximately two years, Russia will pose a credible threat to
one or several NATO countries and thus be ready for a regional war
against several countries in the Baltic Sea region.

e Within approximately five years, Russia will be ready for a
large-scale war on the European continent.

The timeframes stated above remain valid for the three types of war
mentioned. This updated assessment, however, concerns Russia’s
willingness and ability to escalate against the West in the coming
months, either by carrying out more frequent and more severe hybrid
attacks or by carrying out limited military attacks against one or
several NATO countries bordering Russia. Russia could do this even if
the war in Ukraine continues and Russia is not ready for a regional war
or a large-scale war against NATO.

The DODIS applies the below scale of probability

Possible
40-60%

Less likely
10-40%

Likely
60-90%

Highly likely

Highly unlikely
<10% >90%

The probabilities are estimates, not calculated statistical probabilities. “We assess” corresponds to “likely” unless a different probability level is indicated.

The updated assessment supplements DDIS’s 9 February 2025
assessment

On 9February 2025, the DDIS published an assessment of the threat
posed by Russia to the Danish Realm, which expanded on a number of
its assessments of the threat from Russia set out in Intelligence
Outlook 2024.

In the February 2025 threat assessment, the DDIS assessed when
Russia could be ready for different types of war. The timelines
depended on that the war in Ukraine ends or turns into a frozen
conflict, that Russia’s conventional military capabilities continue to
grow while the West fails to simultaneously build up its military
capabilities at the same speed, and that Russia assesses that the
United States cannot or will not support the European NATO countries
in a potential war against Russia:

e Within approximately six months, Russia will be able to wage a local
war in a country bordering Russia.

e Within approximately two years, Russia will pose a credible threat to
one or several NATO countries and thus be ready for a regional war
against several countries in the Baltic Sea region.

e Within approximately five years, Russia will be ready for a
large-scale war on the European continent.

The timeframes stated above remain valid for the three types of war
mentioned. This updated assessment, however, concerns Russia’s
willingness and ability to escalate against the West in the coming
months, either by carrying out more frequent and more severe hybrid
attacks or by carrying out limited military attacks against one or
several NATO countries bordering Russia. Russia could do this even if
the war in Ukraine continues and Russia is not ready for a regional war
or a large-scale war against NATO.
